speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subtopic: CROWSNEST PASS FREIGHT RATES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity namely, that the railway companies are engaged in a national propaganda campaign to abolish the statutory Crowsnest freight rates which have been in existence since 1898 and which have been a cornerstone of benefit to the western wheat farmer and to tens of thousands of farmers who otherwise would have been unable to carry on.
Should the railways be successful in their objective, a body blow will have been struck to western farmers. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn):
That this House declares there shall be no interference with these rates and that they should be continued in full force and effect.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: REDUCED SUBSIDY ON DOMESTICALLY CONSUMED GRAIN-RESULTANT INCREASE IN PRICE OF BREAD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct my question to the Minister of Transport, in his capacity as the minister responsible for the Wheat Board. In 1973, the government responded to an anticipated five-cent increase in the price of a loaf of bread by putting in place a subsidy on domestically consumed wheat. That program was to last for a period of seven years. The Prime Minister said at that time:
In present world conditions the most urgent task of the government is to ensure that those who are least able to defend themselves against the effects of inflation are protected.
Since this will make little or no difference to wheat producers, why is the government now moving to cancel the subsidy and pass a large percentage of the burden to low income families in Canada who have to rely to a very large extent on bread and pasta in this period of rising food prices?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: REDUCED SUBSIDY ON DOMESTICALLY CONSUMED GRAIN-RESULTANT INCREASE IN PRICE OF BREAD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the arrangement made in 1973 was an arrangement with wheat producers that for seven years there would be a certain range within which the returns to them might move in connection with wheat sold for consumption in Canada. That range was originally set between a floor of $3.25 and a ceiling of $5. What we are now proposing is to raise the floor to $4 having regard to changes in the costs of production, and to allow the price to float in that range.
In 1973, because there had already been a very rapid escalation in the price of wheat to the $3 level and through that figure, the government decided to cushion the immediate impact of the rise by paying a consumer subsidy effective on everything over $3.25. That has gone on for some five years, to the benefit, I believe, of consumers to the extent of some $385 million. Now the government has decided that its spending restraint program requires this to be reviewed. Therefore, the cost-which perhaps would have been a cost to the treasury of $100 million this year-will now be changed in terms of a non-spending item and the Wheat Board will be free to make such a charge as the world price would indicate between the $4 and $5 range, which is a continuation of the old agreement.

November 29, 1978
Oral Questions
While there will be an unfortunate, but necessary, increase in the price of bread, it should be recognized that it follows five years of complete stability in the part of the bread price which represents wheat. Other factors have gone up, of course, and the price of bread has continued to rise over that period- but not because of wheat. Now an adjustment is being allowed in relation to wheat which in total will have, I am told, approximately a 0.1 per cent impact upon the cost of living index compared to, say, 0.5 per cent to 0.7 per cent that the oil price increase would have meant.

subtopic: REDUCED SUBSIDY ON DOMESTICALLY CONSUMED GRAIN-RESULTANT INCREASE IN PRICE OF BREAD
speechtext:
Surely the minister knows that that 0.1 per cent increase will lean most heavily on the group in society which needs protection most, that is, low income earners. When that policy was introduced, bread was 36 cents a loaf; it is now 60 cents a loaf. As a result of the government's move, it will go up to 70 cents a loaf by June of next year.
1 ask the minister, why did the government, if they felt it was absolutely necessary as a restraint measure-I think the House and the country would seriously question that-not ease it in over a period of years, as it has done with oil prices, to offset the impact on consumers? Why is the government not doing this in the case of bread, given the impact it will have on poor families in the country who are finding it hard enough as it is to get by?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: REDUCED SUBSIDY ON DOMESTICALLY CONSUMED GRAIN-RESULTANT INCREASE IN PRICE OF BREAD
speechtext:
Lack of action in 1973 would have meant a very high proportionate increase in the price of bread, because bread was priced lower and wheat prices went up to $5.50 at that point. This shows the reason for the change today. As a proportion of bread prices, the increase will be far, far lower than it would have been if that had been allowed to happen in 1973.
However, the answer to the over-all question is that we have to exercise restraint in government spending from the point of view of the over-all impact on the economy of dollars spent by the government, whether through a deficit or through additional taxes. That was an essential program. As part of that program, we are transferring large amounts of money through improved social programs to those who need them most, and hence we put before the House recently the proposal to increase the guaranteed income supplement to older persons. Also, of course, we have the tax credit for families with children under the $18,000 bracket. These people will be helped substantially by these measures.

subtopic: REDUCED SUBSIDY ON DOMESTICALLY CONSUMED GRAIN-RESULTANT INCREASE IN PRICE OF BREAD
speechtext:
I would remind the minister that we also have before the House the Auditor General's report. Perhaps he could look there for a way of implementing restraint, instead of on the backs of the poor.
1 ask the minister whether he consulted his colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, before implementing this move, given the fact that we have already removed this year the consumer subsidy on powdered skim milk in Canada-again, a move which will lean heaviest on low income earners. Did the minister consult the Minister of National

Health and Welfare, and did he satisfy himself about the social impact on low income families in this country of this heartless, Marie Antoinette move which he is now taking?

INCREASE IN PRICE OF BREAD-TWO-PRICE SYSTEM FOR WHEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport and it follows on the questioning of my colleague.
In responding to questions, the minister indicated that this was a kind of floating price plan. Does the minister not recall, when the plan was brought in, that the minister of agriculture at that time said it would enshrine, to use his words, the two-price system for wheat for seven years? He went on to say that it was "a measure to help keep down the cost of bread to Canadians by freezing the price of bread wheat to millers at a maximum of $3.25 per bushel." Would the Minister of Transport now indicate why that word has been broken by defreezing the bread wheat price from $3.25 to $4?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: INCREASE IN PRICE OF BREAD-TWO-PRICE SYSTEM FOR WHEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not a matter of defreezing it from $3.25 to $4. In fact, if the hon. member would check the legislation, he would find that the legislation itself requires a review of the minimum price in the seven-year arrangement having regard to costs of production. Accordingly, last year we increased the minimum from $3.25 to $3.55. This year we are increasing it to $4, much in
November 29, 1978

line with the suggestions made to us by farm organizations about the costs of production.
In 1973, at the same time as we introduced the program of two-price wheat, we introduced a consumer subsidy. We had to change that decision to have a consumer subsidy in relation to bread and wheat, in light of the exact fiscal situation. Surely hon. members will recognize that two-price wheat traditionally has been a program designed specifically in relation to the needs of producers. It is a program for which we from Saskatchewan and other parts of the prairies fought for years until we finally achieved it. It should be seen as a producers' program and not anything else.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when we take the rhetoric away from what the minister has said, once again the government has broken its word to the Canadian public.

speechtext: Dealing with the question of the supposed saving of $100 million-which is a nice way of loading an extra five cents to seven cents on every loaf of bread for Canadian consumers-would the minister indicate if he considered cutting back on some of the losses which are being incurred at Mirabel: $51 million, as pointed out by the Auditor General, and an accumulated loss of $119 million since the airport was opened in 1975? If he considered somehow eliminating those losses, did he not feel that would be a more suitable restraint than to take it out on those in the country who have to eat such a basic commodity as bread?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: INCREASE IN PRICE OF BREAD-TWO-PRICE SYSTEM FOR WHEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know what kind of extraordinary suggestion that is, coming from the hon. member who purports to know something about financing. We have an existing airport. He might wish that it had not been built, but it will prove that it is very badly needed over the next number of years. He might wish that it had not been built, but since the only loss on the airport, effectively, is the carrying of the actual interest charges against the original investment, nothing we do now will change that fact.
The fact of the matter is, money does not appear easily, in terms of savings, for the whole financial account. This government knew, when it was going about the cost-cutting exercise, that it would be cutting a lot of good programs. Even though hon. members opposite always made it sound as though programs could be cut easily and painlessly, we knew that would not be so. We do not like cutting this particular program in relation to the price of bread. But we had to make choices to keep our over-all financial position in order and to avoid the spurring of inflation, which is a very important priority for the government. Therefore, we had to act.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a good deal of the discussion that has taken place on this bill has had to do with the desirability of its benefits being passed on to the families of this country. In that context, quite a bit has been said about the desirability of the provinces not cutting back on any of their benefits because of the benefits provided under this legislation. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has said on two or three occasions that she has made a very strong plea to the provincial governments in that respect, and I hope that by today she may have something to say to the House as to what assurances she has received from the provinces.
Before she rises to comment on that aspect of the matter, I should like to ask her to comment on something else which is in the same vein. As we all agree, it is very important when old age pensioners receive an increase in their pensions that they receive the full benefit of it. The same should apply to any improvement in family allowances, whether it is in the amount of the allowance itself, or in the form of a tax credit which is to be received in April or May of each year.
Today concern has been expressed in the House regarding the rise in the price of bread. This has led to reminders of the rise in the price of milk and other foodstuffs. In view of the desire of the Minister of National Health and Welfare that this money be of benefit to families, a desire which she has expressed by making appeals to the provincial governments, did she do her best to persuade cabinet not to drop that subsidy and let the price of bread rise? If she did not get into that battle with all her clout and influence, I hope she will do so even yet.
There is not much point in granting an increase of a few dollars a month by the provision of the child tax credit and the changes in family allowances if the cost of bread, milk and other basic necessities rises and, as a result, the families of this country lose the benefit before they receive it. That is precisely the situation. The families of the country will find their family allowance cheques reduced in January; they will not receive any money by way of tax credit until April, but in the meantime there is a rise in the price of bread, as there was in the price of milk. What part has the minister played in attempting to get cabinet not to make the unfair decision announced today by the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope the committee will give me a chance to explain the exact state of affairs regarding the
Family Allowances
guaranteed income supplement and the child tax credit. As to the child tax credit, it is time to review the situation. It is an important matter, as has been indicated by hon. members of all parties during the debate.
On October 20 I sent letters to my provincial counterparts urging them to pass on the child tax credit, and clarifying that the credit could be ignored for CAP cost-sharing. On November 16 I sent telexes to all of them. I made further representations and had discussions with them in Toronto at the November 20 and November 21 meeting of welfare ministers. On November 27 I telexed the provinces clarifying that CAP asset guidelines could be waived as required, to permit a full passing on.
At the federal-provincial conference last week, five provincial colleagues officially indicated to me their cabinets are in the process of recommending that their governments pass it on fully. I am referring to the provinces of Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Ontario, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. I have received no official word from the other five provinces, although every one of them is concerned and understands the problem fully.
I have not received the final approval from any province. I have not received word that their cabinets have approved the recommendation. It is time for groups representing the interests of mothers, underprivileged citizens and families in general to request a clarification of the positions of the provincial governments on this matter.
As I have said, it is good politics at no cost to the provinces. It is federal taxpayers' money which will be transferred to individual Canadian families by a program similar to family allowances. We do not think it should become an additional transfer payment to provinces. That viewpoint and philosophy was expressed by all parties in this debate. I invite voluntary associations interested in the development of social policies or my colleagues in parliament to make their views known to their provincial governments.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the fact that the minister is able to report some progress. She has reached the point where she knows that in five provinces the mills are grinding in the right direction. I hope she will stay with it, and that in the end no Canadian family or child will lose the benefit of Bill C-10 because of cutbacks by the provinces.
However, I should like to hear the minister's comments on the other point I raised. I realize she was busy discussing things with her officials so that she would be ready to participate in this debate and perhaps missed my point. This must be a pretty sad day for her. She is the co-pilot of a bill which provides for increases in family income, and on this very day we received an announcement that the price of bread will rise five to seven cents per loaf, on top of increases in the prices of other foodstuffs.
Every time there is an increase in old age pensions, all of us receive letters from pensioners indicating that rent increases or other cost increases are greater than the actual increases they

receive every three months in their old age pensions. In January the cheques mothers receive will be down to $20 per month, and the tax credit will not be in their hands until April or May. In the meantime, the prices of bread and milk as well as other costs of living rise for these people. The entire exercise in which the minister has been engaged can be brought to nought by these other increases.
I am not attempting to persuade the minister into saying that she disagrees with her cabinet colleagues, such as the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board; but we have the right to know whether she has made any effort to persuade cabinet to take other steps, or refrain from taking the wrong steps, so that the benefit of this legislation will not be wiped out before it is on the books.

However, it would not be fair to the Canadian producers of wheat or milk to freeze the prices of these two commodities. That is important. The role of the Minister of National Health and Welfare is to make sure that Canadians who may suffer a bit ultimately are equipped to fight back and accommodate themselves to the new prices by receiving more than the increase in the cost of commodities. Mr. Chairman, I realize it is difficult for one minister of the cabinet to express disagreement with a stand taken by another minister, but I point out to her that today the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, in defence of his announcement, referred to the increase in the GIS and the increase in the family allowance as an excuse for what he had done, which will produce an increase in the price of bread.
I hope I did not give the impression that I thought the increase in the price of bread by itself was going to wipe out the net increase being made available to families through Bill C-10. However, when you take one thing after another-an increase in the price of bread, an increase in the price of milk,

an increase in the price of turkeys, an increase in the price of beef and in everything down the line, including rents and so on-the good move that she has won could be wiped out.
We are getting a little tired of listening to the minister responsible for the Wheat Board giving us excuses like this, and we are getting a little tired of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs telling us that these things are being looked at and monitored. The grand assurance given by the Deputy Prime Minister today was that the increase in the price of bread will be monitored. In the meantime, the benefits that are supposedly being granted by this parliament, on the initiative of the government with this bill, are being cancelled.
I suggest that most of us in this place appreciate the hard battle the minister has waged in the cabinet in this time of restraint to win anything at all; but we call on her to keep up that fight, to keep using her clout and influence to protect the interests of families in all ways. It is not good enough just to give them a net increase in family allowance and then let the government, by action or by inaction, bring about an increase in the cost of living to the medium and low income families of this country, so that in the end they are no better off, if not worse off.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, maybe I should add one thing. Special measures with special consequences, such as the increase in the price of a loaf of bread as a result of the readjustment of the domestic wheat price, are of special concern. However, generally speaking, the increase in the cost of living is met by the indexing of our programs. I am sure the House knows and regrets, as I do, that indexing could not take place for family allowances in this year, and that in addition there is a slight reduction. However, the child tax credit has been indexed and that is a major feature of this bill of great importance. According to the financial projections the child tax credit next year will be $218 per child.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to pursue the questions raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. It had been my intention to pursue them at the outset, but you went, as opposed to our custom, to the NDP first.
Let me say this to the minister and make it very clear. If she does not know this, it is regrettable. The increase in the price of a loaf of bread as a consequence of what her colleague, the minister responsible for the Wheat Board, did yesterday, will be in the neighbourhood of at least seven cents a loaf. I am told that by this time next year, given the ordinary escalation in costs experienced by the bakeries in Canada, it will be up to about six cents-I am sorry, ten cents a loaf. That "six cents" was a Freudian slip. During the great depression that is what a family in Newfoundland had to get by on-six cents a day.
I want to take the minister back to events of 1973. She will recall that the government of the day, albeit a minority government, met here in emergency session to deal with a national rail strike. At that time, in response to the growing concern in the country over the escalation in food prices and the full impact of inflation, which was then beginning to make itself felt in rising food prices, the government came into the House and introduced a subsidy program for the domestic consumption of wheat, the program which the government has cancelled today. At that time a loaf of bread cost 36 cents.
The reason the government brought the program in at that time was to prevent a five-cent per loaf increase in price. The prime minister introduced that program and gave as his rationale the statement that world conditions make it a most urgent task of government to ensure that those who are least able to defend themselves against the effects of inflation are protected. That action was taken at a time when the universal family allowance payment was substantially increased and bread was 36 cents a loaf.
Now, coincidental with another change in the family allowance law, the government does the very opposite; instead of lowering the price of bread, it removes the consumer subsidy. Bread will probably go to 70 cents a loaf, and not only bread. There is also pasta, which is a very important part of the daily diet of low income families. I am referring to pasta in the form
Family Allowances
of macaroni, spaghetti and so on. It is especially important now, given the fact that since 1973 beef prices have escalated considerably.
It is not enough for the minister to try to talk her way around this, as she did in response to questions by my hon. friend. Was she consulted by her colleague about this subsidy program coming off, resulting in increases in the prices of bread and pasta? Has she done studies to satisfy herself as to what this will mean to low income families? My hon. friend has already referred to other price increases, such as the increase in the price of fowl and turkey, which low income people are depending on more and more as the principal source of meat protein due to increases in the price of beef. This whole thing comes at a time when the consumer subsidies on powdered skim milk are eliminated, resulting in an increase in the price of milk. This is a disaster for low income families in this country.
I have great sympathy for the minister. She has been under tremendous pressure since the House started because she has been in the House continuously to deal with her three bills. These bills deal with increases in the GIS, medical funding, which we voted second reading today, and this bill to amend the Family Allowances Act. We have a bill before us which will reduce the number of people eligible for unemployment insurance and a measure which will eliminate the consumer subsidy on domestically consumed wheat.
We also have a situation which was addressed in the House recently whereby the Minister of Agriculture said that there is no way that the increase in the price of turkeys can be justified at this time because there are ample stocks on hand. Yet the price of turkeys is going out of sight. From a survey taken yesterday, I discovered that prices in Canada on turkeys range anywhere from $1.44 to $1.60 per pound. This is a robbing Peter to pay Paul type of situation. I do not understand how the situation has changed.
In 1973 the government responded in a positive way by putting in a program to provide a subsidy on domestically consumed wheat to eliminate an increase in the price of bread. At the same time they brought in a subsidy on liquid milk. These were moves designed to protect the poor against inflation and were coincidental with a measure which parliament considered at that time to change the concept of the family allowance program by increasing substantially the universal amount of family allowance payments.
I repeat, was the minister consulted by the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers? 1 understand that he was the culprit. We are told by the press that the minister responsible for the Wheat Board resisted having his program removed because it would result in an increase in the price of bread, but the president of the economic development board had his way. It seems to me to be patently unjust for the government to be moving in a counter-productive direction to that in which the Minister of National Health and Welfare is trying to move.
I implore the minister to tell the House that she will recommend to her colleagues that they reconsider this move in

It is difficult for a federal minister to obtain a deal from a Pequiste minister whose government wants to break away from Canada. It should be easy for a member who is supposed to know politics as well as the hon. member opposite to accept that. I made representation to Dr. Lazure-a man who usually
Family Allowances

I have taken every opportunity to invite the provinces to take that course of action. Until a few months ago I did not want to provoke provinces into unnecessary confrontation, but I think the time has come for people in the province of Quebec to ask their government for an accounting. That is the spirit in which I informed the House of this passing on to mothers on welfare the full child tax credit.
I should like to take the opportunity the hon. member has given me to answer a few outstanding questions.
On the question of the supposed discrimination against women on the ground of marital status put forward by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands and the hon. member for Egmont, I have answered that already and it is recorded in Hansard. I confirm again that there is no discrimination against women in this bill other than the fact that the cheque goes to the mother instead of to the child or the father. That is a very important feature of the bill and I am very proud of it. It will put in the hands of mothers of poor families $120 million additional cash. That may be discrimination but I do not go for philosophy, I go for the practical realities of life.
As to the second possible discrimination which, if I understood the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands correctly, is the possibility of discrimination against people living common law, I have answered that. If there is discrimination, it should be addressed in the income tax bill as such because it is a basic feature of the bill. I have said that often.
I do not know if it is part of the rules and regulations that I should repeat something ad nauseam. I do not know who this helps, surely not my throat. However, I will repeat this and maybe the hon. member for St. John's East and I will then understand each other.
Common law situations are not recognized for any purposes under the Income Tax Act. That may be right, it may be wrong. The fact is it would be very difficult to control the situation of common-law marriages in many cases, especially in a society where the standards of behaviour have changed, as they have in all of the western world, toward more trial marriages and so on, which is good. However, how do you control such a situation if time is not an element of it?
I am a bit surprised that the hon. member for St. John's East would advocate a change in the sense of a rejection of the family unit as a basis for policy development. I do not know what he has in mind when he suggests that; he did not explain his reasons.
As to the other outstanding questions, I have been able to obtain answers which I will provide through the hon. member for St. John's East to his colleague.
The hon. member for Provencher asked about the administrative cost of family allowances. The total administrative cost of family allowances is $6.25 per family per year, or 52 cents

I want to satisfy myself that their income, by way of estate or otherwise, is taken care of by Revenue Canada the way it should be, not by the loss of their family allowance. Mr. Chairman, I begin by saying that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is a good minister who appears to be on top of her department. She is a progressive minister who is going in the right way. We have said that many times.
The comments made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for St. John's East have been very relevant. While the minister is trying to do something for the ordinary poor people, other arms of government are doing things that will nullify some of the benefits she is trying to bring about. That is a real tragedy.
There are one or two matters I would like to have clarified. The minister knows that between January 1 and April 1 there will be a decrease in family allowances from $25 and some odd cents to $20. There will be a natural decrease despite the fact that some commodities people are buying for their children are going up in price.
There is something the minister said that should be corrected. She does not appear to know the Wheat Board operation very well. She said the withdrawal of the subsidy meant the farmers would be better off. The subsidy does not have anything to do with the farmer. What we are talking about here is a subsidy to the millers. It is part of the two-price wheat legislation that was introduced and became law in September 1973. It was to cover a period of seven years. As the minister in charge of the Wheat Board said, the law would ensure that the price the millers paid for their wheat would stay at $3.25. He gave a commitment that the price would be frozen at that level, which amounts to seven and a half cents for a 24-ounce loaf for seven years, up to 1980. Today he reneged on that promise in the name of restraint.
Some of the things we are saying today are very relevant indeed. While the minister is doing some really good things, and we compliment her for them, her colleague is doing exactly the opposite, making it more tough for the ordinary citizen.
As the hon. member for St. John's East said, and as I said earlier in the debate, the bakery council of Canada has stated that the average price of bread will increase by about seven cent a loaf. This is despite the fact that withdrawal of the subsidy would put the price of wheat up by only 3.3 cents a loaf. The sum of 3.3 cents a loaf in terms of the cost of the raw material will equal 7 cents a loaf in terms of what a person is going to pay for it retail. That is a big increase.
November 29, 1978

The minister said it means only about $10 per family per year, but I would like to have her ask her officials to check their arithmetic. With respect, I think they are wrong. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board said the subsidy was worth $100 million this year, Mr. Chairman. And as I said, you are not just looking at the cost of wheat going up; you are looking at what the miller, the baker, the retailer and the wholesaler are taking in between-up to 7 cents a loaf. The rise will be not 3.3 cents but 7 cents. So if the subsidy at 3.3 cents is worth $100 million, then an increase of 7 cents is worth over $200 million. If you divide the Canadian population into $200 million you come out with about nine dollars for every man, woman and child, or $36 a year for a family of four. That is going to nullify a lot of the good things which are being done by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I don't blame her for that.
I really got to my feet here this afternoon to defend her and to say I wish other ministers were doing what she is doing in terms of looking out for ordinary Canadians. But because the price of bread will rise by about $36 per year per family, a lot of the good things she is doing in terms of raising the family allowance will be nullified.
We also heard her comment that the farmers need price increases. Of course they need price increases, but this lifting of the subsidy will not increase their incomes. Look at turnkeys, for example. The price of turkeys, as the hon. member for St. John's East said, has gone up, in some cases as high as $1.40 or $1.60 a pound. I'll bet you, Mr. Chairman, that whether they sell for $1.60 or $1.40 a pound, the retailer is paying the same wholesale price for those turkeys. I also know that the Canadian turkey producers received only an extra 4 cents this year over last year. So again you have potentially a rip-off by some of the middle men. The ordinary people the minister is trying to help are the ones who will be buying those turkeys for Christmas. We know that 35 to 40 per cent of our turkeys are bought before Christmas, so we can see the impact this will have on those families the minister is trying to help.
These are the points I wanted to make this afternoon. I think they are extremely relevant to the debate. The situation is hypocritical in some ways. We are trying to do something really good on the one hand, and we are appealing to the provinces to make sure that they deduct from their welfare calculations the additional tax credit bonus for children. There are five provinces now which have apparently decided to make that commitment-three Conservative provinces of Newfoundland, New Brunswick and Ontario, the NDP government in Saskatchewan and the Social Credit government in B.C. But there are five which so far have not made any commitment, although I gather from the minister that she is highly optimistic about the province of Quebec where the minister of health is Mr. Denis Lazure. We have gone forcefully to the provinces and said: "Don't count the new family allowance benefits to the kids as income when you calculate welfare payments." We have been able to congratulate the minister for being able to persuade the department of Indian affairs to do the same when
Family Allowances
it comes to the Indian kids on welfare. Yet one of her colleagues, the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, is doing the very thing she is asking the provinces not to do, the very thing parliament is asking the provinces not to do. This seems rather hypocritical to me, as I say.
That is not very good planning. It just does not make sense.
1 think my arguments are very relevant with respect to the debate which is taking place in the House today. It is fine and good to do all these great things, but if they are to be nullified it will just create more cynicism out there among the Canadian population.
There are other things I could mention. It is not just a case of bread or turkey prices, but food prices. The subsidy on skim milk was taken off last year as of March 31. The Minister of Agriculture said consumption of skim milk powder had declined since the subsidy came off. One can see from the studies that low income families consume more skim milk than families with high incomes. It is the low income families with children, particularly those with many children, perhaps five, six or seven, who would normally consume the most skim milk powder of all. They are consuming less of this skim milk powder today because they cannot afford it. This is the question the minister will be forced to face with some of her colleagues in cabinet, particularly the new minister in charge of the economic board who was formerly President of the Treasury Board.
I think we need more planning. We need more social and economic planning within the government. If we do not have it we will just create more and more cynicism out there among the Canadian people.
I am sorry l went on so long, Mr. Chairman, but I thought some of these points were worth making, not as a criticism of the minister but, I suppose, in criticism of a government that does not appear to have its act together and which does not appear to be following the same philosophical road as the minister. Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether the committee is fully aware of the significance of the answer the minister gave to my problem of the orphans. I think it is a very historical occasion when the minister corrects a wrong which has been in existence for six years, namely, discrimination against orphans in Canada. The parliament of this nation, with the support of all parties, passed in 1971 legislation that gave to all children, regardless of the wealth of a family, family allowance of $20 per month per child. Yet when the regulations under that legislation were produced, those regulations barred orphans on the ground that they were adults once their parents died. If your parents had both died, it was said that you must have inherited an estate, and if that estate produced enough money to meet the minimum amount under the Income Tax Act, which several years ago was $1,660-for next year it will be $2,780-you did not receive family allowance.
After five years of effort on my part the minister's word today gave me confidence that there is still hope for our parliamentary system of government. Because after the years of protest from 1974 until now I have finally found a minister who has not just listened and examined the facts and the truth of my statements but is doing something about it. Any person who believes in universal programs and in the universality of this program for family allowances, as this minister does, is duty-bound to tell her colleagues that it is going to be enforced and that the will of parliament is supreme, not the will of those nitwits who make this type of regulation which goes against what parliament has ordered.
I think the minister has established a niche for herself regarding parliamentary procedure. She has courage and conviction. That courage is being used to stand up for what she believes and for what parliament stands for. I accept without any question that what she says is the correct procedure, namely, that under this legislation we are discussing. Bill C-10, the proper procedure is not to amend any part of this legislation. The proper procedure is for the government to amend the regulations under the Family Allowances Act of 1971.
Because there is a monetary consideration at stake, the minister will have to go to the Treasury Board, which accepted these changes when they were brought to its attention. The minister will have to tell her colleagues in the Treasury Board that she has stood up in this House and given her word that the legislation she is putting through is universal as far as children are concerned with regard to the $18,000 provision. The minister has given her word, and as far as she is concerned, what she has said will happen will happen. Then if the

Treasury Board fights her, she has no choice but to go to the Prime Minister and put it in his hands, because the Treasury Board will have overruled not only parliament but also the minister's word in this House.
I think the minister has shown great courage and conviction in relation to something about which she feels very strongly. I am sure every one of us thinks so as well. For seven long years families with young children under 16 years of age have had this hanging over their heads, and they have not even known it. If the parents in a family were to die simultaneously or separately but within a short space of time in an accident of some kind or of natural causes, because both parents were dead their children were not given the benefits of legislation this parliament passed.
The minister has promised to correct that situation in the proper way by changing the appropriate regulation under the Family Allowance Act. Then this legislation she has brought in will be fully operative, because under clause 4 the eligibility is the same as the eligibility under the Family Allowances Act. I am sure the machinery the minister is putting into place for this legislation will handle the problem of orphans. If the total income of a family of orphans is greater than $18,000, that family will follow the same rules as other families. If the income is $18,000 or less, they will follow the same rules as other families earning $18,000 or less and benefit from the negative income tax. I think my concern is completely met.
The significance of this is that when a minister does what this minister has done today, we in this House and all Canadians owe her a great debt of gratitude, not only for her convictions but also for her courage in taking the stand she has taken. Even though mothers and fathers will probably not know what the minister has done, the fact is that some of us here do, and I want to make sure the record shows it. I thank the minister very much.

Mr. Chairman, we are considering that problem. It exists for other Canadian mothers who do not have bank accounts. Often family allowance cheques are cashed in stores which put on special sales around the time of the month when family allowance cheques are received. Often the amount of family allowance cheques can total hundreds of dollars. For example, in the province of Quebec the fourth child and any additional children receive close to $60 each.
Family Allowances
Therefore, the amount of one cheque can easily amount to hundreds of dollars.
I do not think the problem should be made any bigger than it is. It does exist, and we are attempting to see what can be done about it. I would mislead the House if I promised several instalments in the first year of the operation of this program, because it would be technically impossible. The possible problem described by the hon. member can be added to that of tax discounters and family budgeting as reasons for implementing a system of more than one instalment in future years. We are looking into that problem jointly with the National Indian Brotherhood and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I trust people will find ways to cash their cheques easily. I was told that it was not necessarily a big problem.
1 will answer the second part of the hon. member's question as to the general information campaign for all mothers. There was an insert accompanying the October family allowance cheque which gave basic information about the program. There will be another insert in December which will be much simpler in form, consisting of questions and answers and explaining the need for a social insurance number. Accompanying the family allowance cheque for January will be an application form, a Department of National Revenue information sheet explaining how to fill out the form, and a reminder of the need for a social insurance number and how to go about getting one.
At the end of January or the beginning of February there will be a mailing to mothers who are non-filers. The total number of such mothers is approximately 1.5 million, including Indians. It will include a basic income tax form in order to avoid any additional hardship which could be created by the system. In February there will be a reminder to those who have not applied for either social insurance numbers or the benefits. The Departments of National Health and Welfare and Revenue Canada have a joint pamphlet giving basic information about the program. It will be available in all federal offices and, of course, to members of the House. There will be a question and answer guide to that program to inform applicants.
In terms of my own staff, I can confirm that all personnel in regional and local offices in what we call income security, those who look after pension cheques and family allowances, are developing special training for all our officers to help mothers fill in the new forms, in a way similar to the one followed now by our officers in helping elderly citizens. They assist about 60 per cent of all Canadians who fill in GIS forms each year in January, February and March.
What I am developing, and in respect of which I said earlier to the hon. member for Churchill I am not in a position to give more information now, is an information strategy using the local press instead of the national press, something that mothers read. This strategy will eventually involve the use of volunteer organizations, but this is in the making. When I

Mr. Chairman, in a province it is not always easy to be a member of parliament. If the hon. member for Joliette cannot accept that, I do not know what he is doing here. Sometimes in life one must put up a struggle not only against the opposition nor against the government but also against provincial governments whose interests are sometimes opposed to ours. That is very simple. I do not know why he thinks that politics is going to be a big love affair. That is not the way it is. The objectives of provincial governments are not always identical to ours. Their ministers of finance have economic problems just like everyone else. Bill C-10 is a federal bill, concerning a federal program, which uses federal income taxes to redistribute money to families with children, to families in need. As everyone knows in the House, in June 1976 the provinces asked us to look into programs using the tax system to grant supplementary social benefits on a selective basis. We identified three groups, targets which 1 have often discussed in the 14 months since I have been appointed minister, two of which are the poor children of Canada and the single parent families. The provinces are fully aware of the direction in which our work is evolving. At the end of last August, I advised my provincial counterparts of the new program. The best I could do for everyone involved was to introduce a bill, as soon as possible, and giving all the details of the program. Only a bill tells us exactly what we are striving for and what can be changed. What, to my mind, is important and interesting is that none of the provincial ministers suggested any amendments to the bill. All of them told me that they thought the child tax credit program was excellent. Some of them are even a bit envious that they did not introduce it themselves. Or at least, that is what they told me.
Only in the last few years, and I would not be surprised if it were only relatively recently in this House, have hon. members of both the government and the opposition realized that when we approve federal programs dealing with social benefits, particularly for older people, which means increases, whether through quarterly indexing or increases of $20 a month such as the one we just passed for elderly couples and which will start in the month of January, or whether new programs even imperfect such as the spouse's allowance, the provinces take with the left hand what we give individuals with the right hand, in the form of increased rents or more expensive services and so on. It is clear-and federal members of parliament have to fight for that-that the money of Canadian taxpayers

paid out in the form of redistribution, which is the nature of the Canadian confederation as far as I am concerned, when the money of the taxpayers of this country through a program like the child tax credit is used for redistribution to Canadian individuals in need, the provinces cannot consider that as an additional transfer payment and pocket the money.

I need an information document which I almost sleep with because I try so hard to promote this bill in which 1 believe.
Quebec is a particular case, and it is faced with particular problems of adaptation, which I am not entitled to discuss in this House, I think, but since indeed the money comes from the same taxpayers, 1 will talk about it a few minutes to explain my particular position. I did say that minister Denis Lazure has his heart in the right place, the hon. member did hear me well, but then again I am not stupid. I know his government wants to prove that confederation does not work so he will certainly not send me flowers on a silver tray. I mean, there should be no confusion. Having said that, I do not know the recommendation he made to his cabinet, but since the very first time I talked to him, in the evening of August 23 or 24, if my memory serves me well, he has always shown his interest in that program. This, I can confirm, he gave no information about the nature of his recommendations to his cabinet at the federal-provincial conference.
The problem which he faces is unique to the province of Quebec and concerns what they call harmonization. The province of Quebec chose, as it was free to do, a program where

November 29, 1978
Family Allowances
family allowances are distributed differently than in other provinces. Canadians in general receive $25.68 per child every month. Alberta has a somewhat different program, but Quebec has a completely different system about which we were not consulted. This is what the provincial government chose to do, but this is now causing the following problems: Quebec-and 1 hope I am not wrong because this issue comes under the jurisdiction of the National Assembly and I hope that it will be brought up in the proper forum-Quebec gives $15.42 for the first child-and I should say first of all that Quebec asks us to give $15.42 for the first child-the second child in a family receives $23.11, the third child, $47.45, and the fourth and all others receive a cheque of $59.13 a month. Then, there are some adjustments made to increase these amounts if the child is older, that is if he is between 12 and 17 years old.
As I understand it-but once again, I am not the Quebec minister of welfare-Quebec decided to give these welfare payments to mothers who are on welfare only for the first children in a family. Now 1 hope that the hon. member will not be angry with me if I do not know the answer-1 am not the provincial minister-that is if I do not know whether this means the first three children or the first four children. I believe it is only the first three children of a family on welfare who can receive assistance, as well as the mother and the father if it is a two-parent family. The fourth, fifth, sixth and seventh children receive nothing under the welfare program. However, the Quebec government considers that our large family allowance cheque, that it distributes as I described a few minutes ago, will compensate social welfare. Quebec is in a bad position at the present time. I do not know what this means in actual facts for the distribution of welfare costs, of which we must pay 50 per cent, but I do know that the principle of harmonization is suddenly being questioned and that the minister is reconsidering the whole matter.
Of course, many people say that at first sight it seems better to give much more money for the second, the third, the fourth child and so on. But there is a problem of which everyone with children is aware and which governments and especially members of the National Assembly sometimes forget, I think there are not enough women in any of our governments. Even if ours has made some progress in that respect, people forget that the first child costs more money. Essentially, when you have a first child, very often it means, at least in cities, that you must move to have one more bedroom which increases considerably your rent, you have to buy the little bassinet, the bed, diapers, clothing, all the basic equipment. So I consider that the first child should get a larger amount. Furthermore, the second child does not cost much. As everybody knows, he lives on hand-me-downs. According to psychologists, it may be the source of problems but it is another matter. For the third child, many things are worn out and must be replaced. At any event, this is much controversed in circles interested in family policy

matters. This issue is also in the background of discussions in the provincial government cabinet.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 1 deeply dislike the word "illegitimate" children. All children are legitimate. These are words we should not be using. They mean more than the word itself.
As a rule the person who now qualifies for the family allowance receives the new child tax credit. That may be the grandmother, as in the case described by the hon. member for Churchill, or it may be the father, depending on who gets the family allowance. Quite often it also depends on who has legal custody, but this is not necessarily the case.
In the thrust of his question I think the hon. member made a plea for the children of single parent families. They are a vulnerable group. By all standards in 1975, 31.2 per cent of them were poor. Of those, 90 per cent are headed by women. This group will be significantly helped by the new child tax credit. They will receive $106 million in credit payments. To use another measure, 87 per cent of all single parent families in Canada will get total or partial benefits from the new child tax credit.
I think that answers the hon. member's question. If there are particular cases, the officials will be pleased to give answers on a personal basis. I do not know if the hon. member is referring to a particular case.

in family allowance at the first of the year. This should be on record because it is going to be very confusing for many people in our isolated communities.
In committee, I asked the deputy minister of Indian affairs some questions. Even though this question does not pertain to Bill C-10, the department of Indian affairs is responsible for the welfare of Indian people in Canada. It seems there was very little on communication with the department of Indian affairs concerning Bill C-10. At this committee meeting on November 23, I asked the deputy minister what effect Bill C-10 will have on Indian people living on reserves. I quote:
Will the reduction in family allowances be compensated for by an increase in social assistance payments in cases where a family is in receipt of social assistance, I think that is the first order of questioning.
The second question is the adverse of that. What happens to social assistance payments to families that are in receipt of the once a year tax credit.
The deputy minister replied to those questions in this way:
I think I read a transcript of a different exchange between Mr. Smith and the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I do not know whether I can answer all of those questions, but I could make a couple of general observations. Our practice across the country is to conform with respect to social assistance payments to provincial practice, that is, to say we tie ourselves to provincial rates and when the province increases its rates we increase whatever a province's rules may be off reserves we normally apply on reserves.
It is my understanding that in calculating eligibility for social assistance and appropriate levels for social assistance, provinces do not take account of family allowance payments. It would allow from this that since they are excluded from the calculation of the requirements for social assistance, that in your monthly, or whatever, payments, you would neither take cognizance of the reduction in the monthly rate nor of the lump sum payment and the tax credit. The subject is one that is still under discussion between ourselves and the Department of National Health and Welfare. I think it is possible that at some point the two ministers will need to meet to make a determination on some of these issues. It is probably going to be fairly difficult to arrive at firm conclusions about what kind of regime should be applied until we have a picture of what the provinces are likely to do. And in outlining existing practices and the sort of one logical conclusion that you could draw from that practice-I am speaking hypothetically, the subject is not decided, but if we were to conform to our past practice of tying what we do on reserves to what provinces do off reserve, and given the family allowances are excluded from the calculations for requirements for social assistance, then on that particular hypothesis, you would not get an adjustment upwards in the monthly social assistance payment, nor would you get an adjustment downward from the tax credit payment point of view.
The deputy minister said they would not be affected as far as the downward adjustment would be concerned. However, I was concerned about the other adjustment we were talking about. That indicated to me it was not conclusive that the additional welfare would be paid. The minister emphatically says it will be paid and that the individual will not have to pay back any payment that is made to a family now living on welfare because of a drop in income to that particular family. While the minister says this is going to happen, the deputy minister of Indian affairs says that some meetings will have to take place. Perhaps that meeting has taken place since November 23. Can the minister confirm whether that meeting has taken place? If so and it has been decided, there is no point in my going any further.

credit. The next time I will have him at my briefing sessions. I did not know he would be asked these questions. It is a bit unfair.
What I said to the hon. member for Churchill, and I repeat it for the tenth time, is that the minister of Indian affairs and myself have agreed on supplementing any families on welfare wherever it is needed, whatever the method of distribution. There is agreement upon its objective. Of course, the officials will have to work out the particulars, but that is agreed. There is no doubt about it. One of my assistant deputy ministers who is present in the gallery today will clarify this as soon as possible and bring the comments which have been made today to the attention of the deputy minister of the department of Indian affairs.
When the deputy minister of Indian affairs referred to the provincial welfare scales he described the right mechanism. We want to keep a balance for all Canadians. Indian affairs is rather like a provincial department when it comes to social assistance, so we maintain consistency in welfare policies and payments in the country. Provinces, within that general framework, have very different modes of accounting for income. I can possibly say that in fact they all count family allowances as income. I can also say that they don't. It is an accounting practice by which two or three of the provinces count the family allowance one way and the others count it in another way. In any event, it is always taken into account. I wrote to my colleagues and I also told them orally that with respect to any social assistance payments, whatever the accounting practices, they should not count the new child tax credit as income. Nevertheless, it does appear somewhere on the total balance sheet.
It is a bit complicated but it is really a matter for provincial welfare ministers. It may be that the deputy minister of Indian affairs is referring to that mechanism when he speaks of maintaining consistency with the provinces-that may not be the phrase but I do not have the long text which the hon. member read. However, I can assure the hon. member that for the first three months in some families in which there are many children, the decrease in family allowances will mean a manque a gagner, a need, an additional need which will be made up from the payments under Indian affairs. The child tax credit in itself means for Indian mothers in Canada in 1979 an additional net S19 million. The hon. member referred to that at the beginning of his question. For poor families in Canada it means a net additional $108 million taking into account reduction of the family allowance.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext: The usual mechanism will be used to determine who has additional need. That will not increase staff or man-years. We are talking about the first three months of the year. It is quite easy to determine. In most cases this is done with the co-operation of band councils, so it is the same mechanism which will determine additional social assistance needs.

Mr. Chairman, I want to return in my question to my old friends the income tax discounters. I have two questions relating to them. 1 am sure the minister has received a brief from the national anti-poverty organization. I know she will recall from that brief that that organization raised the question of the effect of the lump sum payment on the way mothers who receive this payment will react. In other words, the proposal of the organization was that families at least be given the option of receiving the money four times a year.
I do not want to labour this point because 1 know the minister has already expressed an interest in looking at this matter after the first year of the program. I simply want to ask the minister to remain open and to keep looking at that possibility, because I think there is a severe deficiency in the present approach which is being proposed by the government.
There is another point I want to make with respect to this problem. I was not in the House at the time but I understand that the minister told the House that information is already going out to people with the current family allowance cheques. Is any information going out with respect to the tax credit?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext: The basic information strategy is not yet finished.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
In that case, perhaps my suggestions will have some effect, who knows? Stranger things have happened. I suggest that a pamphlet which is not written in bureaucratese, which includes pictures and which would be lively would be read. Perhaps the minister should consult some of her political advisers in this regard rather than her civil service advisers. Those of us who are in this game know that we have to get information across to people, and I would like to see this information put across to welfare mothers. I intend to do that in my riding in my next household letter. I intend to tell people who will be receiving these cheques that they should wait and that hopefully there will be no need for them to go to income tax discounters.
I return to this point because when the income tax discounting bill was introduced and passed last year, it was suggested that the people who would be seeking income tax discounts

Family Allowances
would be people who would be filling out income tax forms which are complex, difficult and involve some work in filling out. In other words, the people filling out the forms were getting fees for their services as well as straight security for loans.
Let it be said that anybody should be able to fill out the form which is intended to be sent out in January of next year. I hope it is the intention of the government that the form will be very simple and extremely straightforward. Let us hope that it will be a one-page form and that it will be possible for recipients of the forms to fill them out on their own, or they will be counselled to go to community groups, to their members of parliament, to their MPPs or to people who will be filling out forms in relation to the graduated guaranteed income supplement, which the minister knows is filled out at the same time, so they do not have to go to income tax discounters to get the form filled out.
I assure the minister that people in the income tax discounting business are going to be going through housing estates and communities. They will be distributing leaflets telling people that they can get their money quickly. Discounters will be using that commercial approach. I think the government is making a mistake, but let it go ahead. The government is making the mistake of allowing income tax discounters to take this money as security. However, let us at least fight the commercial approach which will be used. Let us undertake that fight with our own public relations efforts.
I hope there will be a public relations effort in which individual members of parliament who feel as strongly as I do about these people will be assisted by the government in seeing that information is provided and that people will have some basic consumer counselling with respect to these forms.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in the few minutes left I want to say that at times I am tempted to agree with the hon. member on the non-assignability of these child tax credit cheques; but I am always reminded-rightly so, it seems to me-of the freedom of people to obtain their money early if they want to.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext: They don't "want" to, they have to.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
It is not a matter of wanting. They do not even know as yet whether that money will be included in their family budgets.
The balance of the hon. member's remarks represented an excellent suggestion which as far as my department is concerned will be implemented. The particular dimension described by the hon. member by which tax discounters help people in filling out difficult forms is very true. Unfortunately, the insert for the month of December is in the process of being printed. It is too late to include the hon. member's suggestions in that insert. However, in subsequent inserts there will be special paragraphs for children which I hope will be "alive".
I can assure the hon. member that the next insert will be the result of advice from my political staff. It will contain pictures and it will be colourful. I hope it will not be boring. There will be pictures of children on it. It will be a small insert which will not tell the whole story, but it will be a beginning. I will supply hon. members with material. I like the idea that members of parliament should conduct clinics in their own constituencies. All the other suggestions made by the hon. member will be explored. I am not sure if the hon. member was in the House earlier, so I will repeat that social workers in all provinces and other provincial officials will also help mothers who are on welfare.
